title: Database connection pool regression in payment-api after v2.9.0
symptoms: HTTP 502 Bad Gateway responses increased immediately after deployment v2.9.0
Spike in gateway timeouts on /v1/charges and /v1/refunds
Downstream services receiving 502 from payment ingress
suspected_cause: Database bottleneck or network blip during rolling deployment
confirmed_root_cause: Database connection pool configuration regression: pool_max was inadvertently decreased from 50 to 5 in v2.9.0 config, leading to connection starvation under standard traffic.
investigation_steps: Monitored HTTP status code distribution on ingress ALB
Compared connection pool configuration between v2.8.4 and v2.9.0 release manifests
Observed exhausted database connection pool metrics in RDS metrics dashboard
Verified active PostgreSQL connections were pegged at pool limit (5)
actions_taken: Initiated immediate rollback of payment-api deployment from v2.9.0 back to v2.8.4
Restored the previous connection pool configuration (pool_max=50)
Monitored database connection count and HTTP 502 error rates
resolution: Rolled back v2.9.0 release and restored previous connection pool configuration parameters.
outcome: Successful. Errors returned to baseline within 2 minutes of rollback completion. No data corruption.
impact: 12 minutes of elevated 502 errors affecting ~8% of payment checkout attempts.
failed_approaches: Initially considered scaling out worker replicas, but realized connection pool per pod was too small and would overwhelm DB backend without fixing config.
successful_approaches: Config diff comparison between release tags v2.8.4 and v2.9.0
Fast rollback rather than in-place patching
engineering_decisions: Roll back immediately rather than testing in-place config edits under active outage.
warnings: Do not attempt pod restarts before inspecting connection pool limits, as restarts will drop active database connections.
lessons_learned: For payment-api 502 errors immediately after deployment, compare database connection pool configuration before restarting infrastructure.

title: Environment variable configuration mismatch on payment-api v2.9.5
symptoms: HTTP 502 errors immediately after deployment v2.9.5
Upstream bank payment gateway requests timing out after 30s
Health check probes intermittently failing on newly deployed pods
suspected_cause: Third-party payment gateway downtime or DNS degradation
confirmed_root_cause: Incorrect environment configuration introduced during deployment: PAYMENT_GATEWAY_TIMEOUT_MS was set to 500ms instead of 5000ms, and upstream auth header variable name was misspelled.
investigation_steps: Checked gateway provider status page and verified external gateway was healthy
Examined application logs for timeout traces
Inspected Kubernetes ConfigMap and Secret diff between v2.9.4 and v2.9.5
Found incorrect environment variables applied during the CI/CD release pipeline
actions_taken: Triggered emergency rollback of deployment to v2.9.4
Corrected the environment variables in the Helm values repository
Re-deployed verified configuration with staging validation
resolution: Rolled back deployment to v2.9.4 and corrected environment configuration.
outcome: Successful. 502 errors cleared immediately upon rollback completion.
impact: 6 minutes of failed transactions for European card processing.
failed_approaches: Contacted external payment gateway support before verifying internal configuration diff.
successful_approaches: Inspecting git diff on environment configuration and Helm release manifests.
engineering_decisions: Enforce automated linting and schema validation on all deployment environment variables.
warnings: Always inspect environment variable and secrets diffs when 502 errors occur within minutes of deployment.
lessons_learned: For payment-api 502 errors following a release, verify environment variable and gateway timeout configurations before assuming external provider downtime.

title: Duplicate payment processing caused by uncoordinated emergency restart
symptoms: Production instability, request latency degradation, and intermittent HTTP 500/504 errors
suspected_cause: Memory leak or locked workers in payment processing pipeline
confirmed_root_cause: Under heavy traffic, workers were slow due to database lock contention. An on-call engineer executed an emergency restart of the payment-api pods while transactions were in-flight, severing active database connections without graceful draining.
investigation_steps: Checked server resource utilization and worker threads
Reviewed pod lifecycle events and restart timestamps in Kubernetes audit logs
Analyzed transaction reconciliation reports indicating identical idempotency keys re-executed across pod restarts
Identified uncommitted 2PC transactions retried by upstream client queues
actions_taken: Halted automated retry queues to prevent further duplicate submissions
Executed database reconciliation script to identify and reverse duplicate authorizations
Notified affected customers and finance team of duplicate authorization holds
resolution: Stopped emergency restarts, allowed pods to drain cleanly, and resolved database lock contention via index optimization.
outcome: Restart temporarily reduced errors but caused duplicate payment processing for a subset of requests. Required 4 hours of manual financial reconciliation.
impact: 47 customer transactions charged twice, $12,400 in duplicate pending authorizations.
failed_approaches: Executing 'kubectl rollout restart deployment/payment-api' as an immediate reflexive fix during active payment traffic without checking in-flight transactions.
successful_approaches: Freezing retry queues and auditing transaction ledger with finance.
engineering_decisions: Establish strict engineering policy forbidding automatic or emergency restarts of payment-api without drain verification.
warnings: CRITICAL: Do not blindly restart payment-api during payment incidents. Sudden restarts sever in-flight transactions and induce retry storms that create duplicate charges.
lessons_learned: Do not blindly restart payment-api during payment incidents. Graceful draining and idempotency guarantees must be verified before cycling payment services.

title: Engineering Decision: payment-api restart policy
symptoms: High latency, elevated 5xx errors, or perceived service hang
investigation_steps: 1. Check deployment changelog and release diffs from recent deployments
2. Inspect database connectivity, active connection count, and connection pool saturation
3. Inspect environment variables, timeout thresholds, and upstream credentials
4. Verify queue lag and downstream gateway health before touching service lifecycle
actions_taken: Formalized engineering standard in runbooks and CI/CD operations manual
resolution: Adopted mandatory operational rule prohibiting emergency restarts without lead SRE sign-off and drained queues.
outcome: Zero duplicate charge incidents recorded since policy adoption.
impact: Protects payment ledger integrity across all production incidents.
failed_approaches: Treating payment-api as a stateless service that can be freely restarted.
successful_approaches: Root-cause diagnosis focusing on configuration, pool limits, and upstream timeouts first.
engineering_decisions: Do not automatically restart payment-api during production incidents.
Reason: A previous emergency restart (INC-1091) caused duplicate payment processing.
Preferred approach: Investigate deployment changes, database connectivity, connection pools, and configuration before restarting the service.
Risk: Automatic restart can worsen payment consistency problems.
warnings: AUTOMATIC OR REFLEXIVE RESTART PROHIBITED: Restarting payment-api under load risks data loss and duplicate customer charges.
lessons_learned: Payment services require strict transactional consistency. Always investigate configuration and connection pools rather than restarting infrastructure.

title: Elevated 5xx errors in orders-api after deployment due to misconfigured environment variable
symptoms: Elevated 5xx errors (HTTP 500 and 503) after deployment v1.14.2
Order placement endpoint /orders failing for all checkout flows
Application pod logs reporting 'Invalid configuration key: INVENTORY_SERVICE_PORT'
suspected_cause: Inventory service outage or network partition between orders and inventory clusters
confirmed_root_cause: Bad environment variable configuration: INVENTORY_SERVICE_PORT was set to string 'http' instead of integer '8080' during helm template rendering.
investigation_steps: Checked inventory service status and confirmed it was running normally
Inspected container logs for stack traces showing startup and runtime parse errors
Compared environment variables between v1.14.1 and v1.14.2 in deployment manifests
Identified bad port format in ConfigMap
actions_taken: Rolled back orders-api to v1.14.1 deployment manifest
Corrected the port specification in helm values for v1.14.2
Validated order creation in staging and re-deployed
resolution: Rollback and correct configuration in deployment parameters.
outcome: Successful. Errors dropped to zero within 90 seconds of rollback.
impact: 8 minutes of order submission failure, approximately 110 blocked orders.
failed_approaches: Investigating inventory service cluster when the defect was localized to the orders-api configuration.
successful_approaches: Diffing environment variables between previous known-good release and current release.
engineering_decisions: Add strict type checking and CI schema validation for all numeric environment variables.
warnings: Always check container logs for configuration validation errors immediately after deployment.
lessons_learned: For post-deployment 5xx spikes, compare environment/configuration changes against the previous known-good release.
